response:
A public library considering facial-recognition checkout is making a small operational choice with disproportionately large symbolic and civil-liberties stakes. Worth unpacking carefully.

The benefits are real but modest. Self-checkout is faster, lines shrink, patrons who've lost their card can still borrow, and staff time shifts from scanning barcodes to actually helping people. For elderly or disabled patrons who fumble with cards, recognition is genuinely friendlier. None of those wins are trivial.

The risks are larger than the benefits suggest at first glance, for three reasons specific to libraries.

First, libraries occupy an unusual civic position: they are one of the few places where a person can read about controversial ideas — political dissent, addiction recovery, immigration status, gender transition, abuse hotlines — without identifying themselves. The card system already creates a record, but library reading records have strong legal protections in many jurisdictions and aren't continuously tied to a biometric. Layering a face template onto every checkout permanently links a patron's physical presence to their reading history in a way that's much harder to revoke than a card.

Second, facial-recognition systems still have unequal error rates across skin tone, age, and gender. A library's job is to serve everyone, and an authentication system that fails more often for some patrons than others undermines that mission even when failures are "only" inconvenience.

Third, biometric data is uniquely permanent. A leaked card number can be reissued; a leaked face template cannot. Vendor breaches, government subpoenas, and corporate acquisitions all become threats against patrons who never explicitly consented to permanent biometric storage.

Safeguards that would meaningfully change the picture: (1) the system is fully opt-in, with the existing card-based path preserved and not made noticeably slower as a nudge; (2) face templates are stored locally on library hardware, not on a vendor cloud; (3) templates are non-reversible mathematical embeddings rather than images, with no link back to checkout records once authentication completes; (4) the library publishes an annual transparency report and commits not to share data with law enforcement absent a specific warrant; (5) an independent audit of demographic accuracy is required before deployment and yearly after; (6) a written, easy deletion path lets a patron remove their template at any time.

Balanced recommendation: don't deploy. The throughput gain is small, the symbolic cost to a free-reading institution is large, and a well-designed mobile-card or PIN system captures most of the convenience without introducing biometrics. If the library has already committed to the technology — say, because a city contract pushed it — then deploy only with the full safeguard list above and an explicit sunset clause that forces a public review in two years. Libraries are precisely the institution where the burden of proof should sit on the surveillance technology, not on the patron declining it.
